passages.original: Quanquam Euse- bius Pamphili in decem Ecclesiasticae Historiae li- bris maximo nobis adjumento fuerit, et singulorum, de quibus scripturi sumus, volumina aetates auctorum suorum saepe testentur. Itaque Dominum Jesum Chri- stum precor, ut quod Cicero tuus, qui 824 in arce Romanae eloquentiae stetit, non est facere dedigna- tus in Bruto, oratorum Latinae lingue texens cata- logum, id ego in ejus Ecclesiae scriptoribus 1 enu- merandis, digne cohortatione tua impleam.
passages.english: And yet Eusebius Pamphili, in the ten books of his Ecclesiastical History, has been of the greatest help to us, and the volumes of the individual [writers] about whom we are going to write often bear witness to the dates of their authors. And so I pray the Lord Jesus Christ that what your Cicero, who stood on the citadel of Roman eloquence, did not disdain to do in the Brutus, weaving a catalogue of the orators of the Latin language, I may accomplish worthily of your exhortation in enumerating the writers of His Church.
passages.notes: Numerals such as "824" and "1" are page and footnote marks and have been omitted.

passages.original: Huic soli licitum erat 12 ingredi Sanctu sanctorum : siquidem vesti- bus laneis non utebatur, sed lineis, solusque in- grediebatur templum, et fixis genibus pro populo deprecabatur, in tantum, 832 ut camelorum duritiem traxisse1 ejus genua crederentur. » Dicti et alia multa 2, quae enumerare longum esset. Sed et Josephus 3 in vicesimo libro Antiquitatum refert, et Clemens in septimo Υποτυπώσεων, mortuo Festo, qui Judaeam regebat, missum esse a Nerone successorem ejus Albinum, qui cnm necdum ad provinciam pervenisset, Ananus 4, inquit, pontific, adolescens, Anani filius, de genere sacerdotali, accepta occasione άναρχίας, concilium congregavit, et compellens publice Jacobum, ut Christum Dei Filium denegaret, contradicentem, lapidari jussit.
passages.english: To him alone was it permitted to enter the Holy of Holies, since he did not use woollen garments but linen ones, and he alone used to enter the temple and, on bended knees, pray for the people, so much so that his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of a camel's." He says many other things too, which it would take long to list. But Josephus too, in the twentieth book of the Antiquities, and Clement in the seventh of the *Hypotyposeis* [Outlines], report that when Festus, who governed Judaea, had died, Nero sent Albinus as his successor; and before he had yet reached the province, "Ananus," he says, "the high priest, a young man, son of Ananus, of priestly family, seizing the opportunity of the *anarchia* [absence of government], assembled a council, and publicly pressing James to deny that Christ was the Son of God, when he refused, ordered him to be stoned."
passages.notes: "Sanctu" read as "Sancta"; "cnm" as "cum"; "pontific" as "pontifex".

passages.original: uda vestimenta extorqueri solent 6, in cerebro percussus interiit. Tradit item Josephus, tantae cum sanctitatis fuisse et celebritatis in populo, ut propter ejus necem, creditum sit subversam esse Hierosolymam 7. Hic est de quo Paulus apostolas scribit ad Galatas : Alium autem apostolorum vidi neminem, nisi Jacobum fratrem Domini (Galat. I, 19). Et apostolorum super hoc crebrius Acta testantur (Act. I, 13; XXI, 18; XV, 13). Evange- lium quoque quod appellatur secundum Hebraeos 8, et a me nuper in Graecum Latinumque sermonem translatum est, quo et Origenes saepe utitur, post resurrectionem Salvatoris refert : « Dominus au- tem cum dedisset sindonem 1 servo sacerdotis, ivit ad Jacobum, et apparuit 2. Juraverat enim Jaco- bus, se non comesturum panem ab illa hora 833 qua biberat calicem Domini, donec videret eum resurgentem 3 a dormientibus.
passages.english: …[with which] wet clothes are usually wrung out, he was struck on the head and died. Josephus likewise relates that he was of such holiness and such renown among the people that it was believed Jerusalem was overthrown because of his killing. This is the one of whom the apostle Paul writes to the Galatians: "But I saw none of the other apostles except James the brother of the Lord" (Gal. 1:19). And the Acts of the Apostles frequently bear witness about this (Acts 1:13; 21:18; 15:13). The Gospel too which is called "according to the Hebrews," which I recently translated into Greek and Latin, and which Origen also often uses, relates after the Saviour's resurrection: "But the Lord, when he had given the linen cloth to the servant of the priest, went to James and appeared [to him]. For James had sworn that he would not eat bread from that hour in which he had drunk the cup of the Lord until he saw him rising from among those who sleep."
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-sentence (the fuller's club "with which" wet clothes are wrung). "Calicem Domini" may be the Lord's cup at the Last Supper; some propose a reading in which James drank the cup of the Lord. Footnote numerals omitted.

passages.original: Scripsit au- tem novem ad septem Ecclesias epistolas, ad Ro- manos unam, ad Corinthios duas, ad Galatas unam, ad Ephesios unam, ad Philippenses unam, ad Co- lossenses unam, ad Thessalonicenses duas, praeter- ea ad discipulos suos 7, Timotheo duas, Tito unam, Philemoni unam. Epistola autem quae fertur ad Hebraeos, non ejus creditur, propter styli ser- monisque dissonantiam 8, sed vel Barnabae, juxta Tertullianum 1, vel Lucae evangelistae, 839 juxta quosdam 2, vel Clementis 3 Romanae postea Eccle- siae episcopi, quem aiunt ipsi adjunctum sententias Pauli proprio ordinasse et ornasse sermone. Vel certe quia Paulus scribebat ad Hebraeos, et propter invidiam sui apud eos nominis, titulum in princi- pio salutationis amputaverit 4.
passages.english: He wrote nine epistles to seven churches: one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians, two to the Thessalonians; and besides these, to his disciples, two to Timothy, one to Titus, one to Philemon. But the epistle which is called To the Hebrews is not believed to be his, because of the difference of style and language, but either Barnabas's, according to Tertullian, or Luke the evangelist's, according to some, or Clement's, afterwards bishop of the church of Rome, who, they say, being associated with him, arranged and adorned Paul's thoughts in his own language. Or else, since Paul was writing to the Hebrews, and because of the unpopularity of his name among them, he cut off the title at the beginning of the salutation.

For how could it be that the inseparable companion of the Apostle should have been ignorant of this alone among his other affairs? Moreover Tertullian, who lived near those times, reports that a certain presbyter in Asia, a *spoudastēs* [devoted admirer] of the apostle Paul, convicted before John of being the author of the book, and having confessed that he did it out of love for Paul, was removed from his office. Some suspect

passages.original: Reliquae nutem duae, quarum principium est : Senior Electoe dominoe et natis ejus, et sequentis : Senior Caio charissimo, quem ego diligo in veritate, Joannis presbyteri 2 asseruntur, cujus et hodie alterum 3 sepulerum apud Ephesum ostenditur, etsi nonnulli 5 putant duas memorias 6 ejusdem Joannis evange- listae esse, super qua re cum per ordinem ad Pa- piam auditorem ejus ventum fuerit, disseremus. Quarto decimo igitur anno, secundum post Nero- nem persecutionem movente Domitiano 7, in Pat- mos insulam relegatus, scripsit Apocalypsim, quam interpretatur Justinus Martyr et Irenaeus 8. Interfecto autem Domitiano, et actis ejus ob ni- miam crudelitatem a senatu rescissis, sub Nerva principe 9 redit Ephesum, ibique usque ad Traja- num principem perseverans 1, totas Asiae fundavit rexitque Ecclesias, et confectus senio, sexagesimo octavo post passionem Domini anno mortuus 2, juxta eamdem urbem sepultus est.
passages.english: But the remaining two, of which the beginning [of one] is "The elder to the elect lady and her children," and of the following "The elder to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth," are claimed to be by John the presbyter, whose other tomb is shown to this day at Ephesus, although some think there are two memorials of the same John the evangelist; on which matter we shall discourse when in due order we come to Papias his hearer. So in the fourteenth year, when Domitian raised the second persecution after Nero, he was banished to the island of Patmos and wrote the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr and Irenaeus interpret. But after Domitian was killed and his acts were annulled by the senate because of his excessive cruelty, under the emperor Nerva he returned to Ephesus, and remaining there until the emperor Trajan, he founded and governed all the churches of Asia; and worn out by old age, he died in the sixty-eighth year after the Lord's passion, and was buried near that same city.
passages.notes: "nutem" read as "autem".

There are also attributed to him three volumes to Autolycus, and one treatise against the heresy of Hermogenes, and other short books pertaining to the edification of the Church.

passages.original: Modestus et ipse sub imperatore M. Antonino et L. Aurelio Commodo, adversum Marcionem scripsit librum 8, qui usque hodie perseverat. Feruntur sub nomine ejus et alia syntagmata, sed ab eruditis quasi ψευδόγραφα repudiantur.
passages.english: Modestus also, under the emperor M. Antoninus and L. Aurelius Commodus, wrote a book against Marcion, which survives to this day. Other treatises (syntagmata) are also circulated under his name, but they are rejected by the learned as spurious (pseudographa).
passages.notes: The '8' after 'librum' is a footnote mark and has been omitted.

passages.original: Meminit autem, in Stromatibus suis, voluminis Tatiani adversus gentes, de quo supra diximus, et Casiani 4 cujusdam χρονογραφίας, quod opusculum 5 invenire non potui. Necnon et de Judaeis Aristobu- um 6 quemdam et Demetrium et Eupolemum scri- ptores adversus gentes refert, qui in similitudinem Josephi άρχαιογονίαν Moysi et Judaicae gentis asse- verant. Exstat Alexandri Hierosolymorum episcopi, qui cum Narcisso postea rexit Ecclesiam, epistola super ordinatione Asclepiadis confessoris ad Antio- chenses, congratulantis eis, in qua ponit in fine 7 : « Haec vobis, domini ac fratres, scripta transmisi per Clementem beatum presbyterum, virum illu- sirem et probatum, quem vos quoque scitis, et nunc plenius recognoscetis, qui cum huc venisset juxta providentiam et visitationem Dei, confirma- vit et auxit Domini Ecclesiam.» Constat, Origenem hujus fuisse discipulum.
passages.english: He mentions, in his Stromata, the volume of Tatian Against the Gentiles, of which we spoke above, and the *Chronographia* of a certain Casianus, a little work which I have not been able to find. He also refers to certain Jewish writers against the gentiles, Aristobulus, Demetrius and Eupolemus, who, after the manner of Josephus, assert the *archaiogonia* [antiquity of origin] of Moses and the Jewish nation. There survives a letter of Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, who later governed the church together with Narcissus, to the Antiochenes concerning the ordination of Asclepiades the confessor, congratulating them, in which he writes at the end: "These things, lords and brothers, I have sent you in writing by Clement the blessed presbyter, a distinguished and approved man, whom you also know and will now come to know more fully, who, when he came here according to the providence and visitation of God, strengthened and increased the Church of the Lord." It is agreed that Origen was his disciple.
passages.notes: "Casiani" is presumably Julius Cassianus. "Aristobu- um" read as "Aristobulum".

Through his zeal, expense and urging Origen sent out a great many treatises to him.

passages.original: Julius Africanus 8, cujus quinque de Tempo- ribus exstant volumina, sub imperatore 9 M. Au- relio Antonino, qui Macrino successerat, legatio- nem pro instauratione urbis Emmaus su cepit, quae postea Nicopolis 10 appellata est. Hujus est epistola ad Origenem super quaestione Susannae : eo quod dicat in Hebraeo hanc fabulam 1 non ha- beri, nec convenire cum Hebraica etymologia άτΧ τού σχίνου σχίσαι2, καί άπδ του πρίνου πρι- σαι, contra quem doctam epistolam3 scribit Ori- genes. Exstat ejus ad Aristidem altera epistola, in qua super διαφωνίφ, quae videtur esse in ge- nealogia Salvatoris apud Matthaeum et Lucam, plenissime disputat.
passages.english: Julius Africanus, whose five volumes On the Times survive, under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, who had succeeded Macrinus, undertook an embassy for the restoration of the city of Emmaus, which was afterwards called Nicopolis. His is a letter to Origen on the question of Susanna, in which he says that this story is not found in the Hebrew, and does not agree with the Hebrew etymology of "from the mastic tree [he will] cleave" and "from the holm-oak [he will] saw"; against him Origen writes a learned letter. There survives another letter of his to Aristides, in which he discusses very fully the discrepancy which seems to exist in the genealogy of the Saviour in Matthew and Luke.
passages.notes: The Greek phrases are the puns in Susanna (schinos/schisai, prinos/prisai), which Africanus argued could not exist in Hebrew. Footnote numbers from the printed page have been omitted; "su cepit" read as "suscepit".

passages.original: Έστι κσ\ έπιστολή πρός Ώριγέ- νην, Ινεχεν τής κατά Σωσάνναν ζητήσεως · λέγει γάρ έν τώ Έβραικψ τούτον μή είναι τδν μύθον, μηδέ τη Έβραίκή άπδ τού πρίνου πρίσαι, κα\ άπδ τού σχίνου σχίσαι, πρδς δν βεδοκιμασμένην έπιστολήν γράφει'Ωριγένης. Έστιν αύτού καϊ πρϊς Άριστείδην άλλη έπι στολή, έν ή περ\ τής διαφωνίας τής δοκούσης είναι έν τη γενεά- λογίφ τού Σωτήρος παρά Ματθαίου κα\ Λουκά άρ- κούντως διαλέγεται.
passages.english: There is also a letter to Origen concerning the inquiry about Susanna; for he says that this story is not in the Hebrew, nor [does it agree] with the Hebrew [the play on] "from the holm-oak to saw" and "from the mastic tree to cleave"; against him Origen writes an approved letter. There is also another letter of his to Aristides, in which he discusses adequately the discrepancy which seems to exist in the genealogy of the Saviour in Matthew and Luke.
passages.notes: This is the Greek version of Jerome's text printed alongside the Latin; the Greek text is garbled by scanning in places. A verb such as "agree" seems to have dropped out after "Hebrew"; supplied in brackets.

passages.english: Theodore, who was later called Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea, while still quite young, for the sake of education in Greek and Latin letters, crossed from Cappadocia to Berytus, and from there to Caesarea in Palestine, together with his brother Athenodorus. Origen, having seen their exceptional natural ability, urged them to [the study of] philosophy, and, gradually leading them into the faith of Christ, made them his own followers. So, having been taught by him for five years, they are sent back to their mother; and Theodore, on departing, wrote a panegyric of thanksgiving to Origen, and, calling together all the local people, with Origen himself present, he read this oration aloud, which survives to the present. He also wrote a paraphrase of Ecclesiastes, a very short but most admirable work, and other
passages.notes: Greek version of Jerome's chapter on Gregory Thaumaturgus; the sentence continues in the following context ("many letters..."). "ἔκφρασιν" probably for μετάφρασιν/paraphrase.

passages.original: Cornelius, Romanae urbis episcopus, ad quem ocio Cypriani exstant epistolae, scripsit epistolam ad Fabium 1 Antiochenae Ecclesiae episcopum, de synodo Romana, Italica, Africana, et aliam de No- vatiano 2, et de his qui lapsi sunt; tertiam de gestis synodi (Romanoe an. 251); quartam ad eum-·
passages.english: Cornelius, bishop of the city of Rome, to whom eight letters of Cyprian survive, wrote a letter to Fabius, bishop of the church of Antioch, concerning the Roman, Italian and African synod, and another concerning Novatian and those who had lapsed; a third concerning the proceedings of the synod (the Roman [synod] of the year 251); a fourth to the same
passages.notes: "ocio" read as "octo" (eight). The parenthesis "(Romanae an. 251)" appears to be an editorial insertion, not Jerome's. The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: Cyprianus Afer, primum gloriose rhetoricam docuit; exinde suadente presbytero Caecilio, a quo et cognomentum sortitus est, Christianus factus, omnem substantiam suam pauperibus erogavit, ac post non multum temporis electus in presbyterum 5, etiam episcopus Carthaginiensis constitutus est.
passages.english: Cyprian, an African, first taught rhetoric with distinction; then, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius, from whom he also took his surname, he became a Christian, gave all his property to the poor, and not long afterwards, having been chosen as a presbyter, was also made bishop of Carthage.

passages.original: Sed et in duo- decim Prophetas viginti quinque Εξηγήσεων Orige- nis 4 volumina, manu ejus exarata reperi, quae tanto amplector et servo gaudio, ut Croesi opes habere me credam. Si enim laetitia est, unam epistolam habere martyris, quanto magis tot millia versuum, quae mihi videtur sui sanguinis signasse vesti- giis 5 l Scripsit, antequam 6 Eusebius Caesa- riensis scriberet. Apologeticum pro Origene 7, et passus est Caesareae Palaestinae sub persecutione Maximini 8.
passages.english: Moreover I found twenty-five volumes of Origen's Commentaries on the Twelve Prophets, written out in his [Pamphilus's] hand, which I embrace and guard with such joy that I believe I possess the wealth of Croesus. For if it is a joy to have a single letter of a martyr, how much more so many thousands of lines, which he seems to me to have marked with the traces of his own blood! Before Eusebius of Caesarea wrote, he wrote an Apology for Origen, and he suffered [martyrdom] at Caesarea in Palestine in the persecution of Maximinus.
passages.notes: The stray "l" after "vestigiis" read as an exclamation mark.

Εί γάρ μεγίστης έστί χαρμόσυνης μίαν έπιστολήν μάρτυρος Ιχειν, πόσψ μάλλον τοσαύτας χιλιάδας στίχων, δι* ών, ώς έμο\ δοκεΤ, τά f/ νη τού οίκε ίου καταλέλοιπε πάθους! Έγραψε δέ πρδ τού Ευσέβιον συγγράψαι Απολο- γητικήν υπέρ Ώριγένους, κα\ έπαθεν έν Και- σαρεία της Παλαιστίνης έν τω Μαξιμίνου διω- γμψ.
passages.english: [On] the Twelve Prophets twenty-five volumes of Origen's Commentaries, written in his hand, [I] found, which I embrace and guard with such joy that I believe I have the wealth of Croesus. For if it is the greatest joy to have one letter of a martyr, how much more so many thousands of lines, in which, as it seems to me, he has left the traces of his own suffering! He wrote, before Eusebius composed [his], an Apology for Origen, and he suffered at Caesarea in Palestine in the persecution of Maximinus.
passages.notes: Greek version of the Latin; the passage begins mid-sentence (the context ends "and on"). "τά f/ νη" read as "τὰ ἴχνη" (traces). "εὕραν" apparently for "εὗρον".

passages.original: Pierius, Alexandrinae Ecclesiae presbyter, sub Caro et Diocletiano principibus, eo tempore quo eam Ecclesiam Theonas·9 episcopus regebat, floren- tissime docuit populos, et in tantam sermonis di- versorumque tractatuum, qui usque hodie exstant 10, venit elegantiam, ut Origenes junior vocaretur. Constat hunc mirae άσχήσεως et appetitorem vo- luntariae paupertatis fuisse 1, scientissimum et dia- lecticae et rhetoricae artis, 917 et post persecutio- nem omne vitae suae tempus Romae fuisse versatum.
passages.english: Pierius, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, under the emperors Carus and Diocletian, at the time when bishop Theonas governed that church, taught the people with great success, and attained such elegance of speech and of various treatises, which survive to this day, that he was called the younger Origen. It is agreed that he was [a man] of remarkable asceticism and a seeker after voluntary poverty, most learned in the arts of dialectic and rhetoric, and that after the persecution he spent the whole remaining time of his life at Rome.

passages.english: Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre, [a writer] of brilliant and well-composed style, composed books against Porphyry, and a Symposium of Ten Virgins, an excellent work On the Resurrection against Origen, against the same On the Pythoness, and On Free Will, Commentaries on Genesis and on the Song of Songs, and many other works widely read.
passages.notes: Greek version. "Τόρου" read as "Τύρου" (Tyre); "Αλματα των θαμάτων" as "Ἄισματα τῶν ᾀσμάτων" (Song of Songs); "Ιΐυθωνίσσης" as "Πυθωνίσσης" (the medium of Endor).

Ε!σ\ τούτου συγγράμματα περίΤυχής, περί Έγγαστριμύθου κατά Ώριγένους, κα\ άλλαι πολλα\ έπιστολα\, &ς άπαριΟμεΓσΟαι πε- ρισσόν.
passages.english: Eustathius, a Pamphylian by birth, from Side, governed first the church at Beroea in Syria and then [that of] Antioch; having composed much against the doctrine of the Arians, he was banished under the emperor Constantius to Trajanopolis in Thrace, where he is buried. There are writings of his On the Soul, On the Ventriloquist [Medium] against Origen, and very many other letters, which it would be superfluous to enumerate.
passages.notes: Greek version. "θρ£Χϊ1:» 1ν ί" read as "Θρᾴκης, ἐν ᾗ" (of Thrace, where). Jerome's Latin has Constantius here, though historically the exile was under Constantine.

passages.original: 935 Victorinus, natione Afer, Romae sub Con- stantio 5·principe rhetoricam docuit 6, es in extrema senectute, Christi 7 se tradens fidel, scripsit adver- sus Arium libros more dialectico valde obscuros, qui nisi ab eruditis non intelliguntur 8, et Com- mentarios 9 in Apostolum.
passages.english: Victorinus, an African by birth, taught rhetoric at Rome under the emperor Constantius, and in extreme old age, giving himself to the faith of Christ, wrote books against Arius in the dialectical manner, very obscure, which are understood only by the learned, and Commentaries on the Apostle.
passages.notes: The numerals (935, 5–9) are column and footnote marks and have been omitted. 'es' read as 'et', 'fidel' as 'fidei'. 'The Apostle' means Paul.

passages.original: 948 Priscillianus 8, Abilae episcopus, qui fa- ctione Hydatii et Ithacii 9 Treveris a Maximo ty- ranno caesus est, edidit multa opuscula 10, de quibus ad nos aliqua pervenerunt. Hic usque hodie a nonnullis Gnosticae, id est Basilidis et Marci 11, de quibus Irenaeus scripsit, haereseos accusatur, de- fendentibus aliis, non ita cum sensisse, ut argui- tur·
passages.english: Priscillian, bishop of Abila, who through the faction of Hydatius and Ithacius was put to death at Trier by the tyrant Maximus, published many short works, of which some have come down to us. To this day he is accused by some of the Gnostic heresy, that is, [the heresy] of Basilides and Mark, about whom Irenaeus wrote, while others defend [him, saying] that he did not hold the views of which he is accused.
passages.notes: The leading '948' is a page or column number, and the figures 8–11 are footnote marks; all are omitted. 'cum sensisse' is read as 'eum sensisse' (scanning error). 'Abilae' is the edition's reading for Priscillian's see; Priscillian is usually known as bishop of Ávila (Abula) in Spain.
